tomato_healthy.description: Foliage exhibits vibrant emerald green composite leaves, crisp turgid leaf stems, symmetrical leaflets, and zero necrotic spotting, marginal chlorosis, or viral mosaic patterns.
symptoms: Lush, uniform green leaflets with well-defined serration
Erect stems with healthy trichomes (hairs) and robust flower trusses
Absence of yellow halos, target-like concentric rings, or mosaic mottling
causes: Optimal soil pH (6.0 - 6.8) with high organic matter
Consistent moisture regime and balanced plant nutrition
Proper trellising and sucker pruning providing exceptional airflow

organic: Apply weekly preventative sprays of biological products (such as Bacillus amyloliquefaciens or Serenade ASO)
Use diluted cold-pressed neem oil (0.5%) to deter aphid and whitefly vectors
chemical: No chemical fungicides or bactericides required for healthy foliage

fertilizer: Supply 5-10-10 or 4-18-38 balanced tomato hydroponic/soil formula with calcium and magnesium
Maintain calcium availability (calcium nitrate or gypsum) to prevent blossom end rot
Limit high-ammoniacal nitrogen during flowering to promote fruit set rather than excessive vine growth
irrigation: Deliver 1.5 - 2.0 inches of water per week using drip emitters placed 6 inches from the plant stem
Irrigate deeply and consistently to maintain root zone moisture tension between -15 and -25 kPa
Never wet foliage; maintain plastic or organic straw mulch to keep leaves completely dry
prevention: Plant indeterminate vines with sturdy stakes, Florida weave, or trellises to elevate vines 4-6 feet above soil
Maintain 18-24 inch plant spacing within rows and 36-48 inches between rows
Prune the lowest 12-18 inches of foliage once vines are 3 feet tall to prevent soil-splash pathogen transmission
recovery_tips: Sanitize pruning tools with 70% isopropyl alcohol between each individual plant
Mulch soil bed immediately after transplanting with clean straw or black plastic

tomato_bacterial_spot.description: A devastating bacterial disease affecting leaves, stems, and fruit. Foliar lesions begin as tiny water-soaked circular to angular dark spots that turn brown/black, frequently bordered by distinct chlorotic halos. Centers of spots may dry out and crack open.
symptoms: Small, angular, dark brown to black water-soaked lesions (less than 3 mm) on foliage
Lesions surrounded by prominent yellow halos, often concentrated near leaf margins
Severe infections cause defoliation of lower canopy exposing green fruits to sunscald
Raised, scab-like, blistered spots on green fruit surfaces
causes: Warm temperatures (25-30°C) with continuous high humidity or frequent overhead irrigation/rain
Bacteria splashing from soil or neighboring diseased seedlings via rain drops
Contaminated seed stock or infected transplant seedlings

severity_rules.mild: < 10% coverage; isolated pinhead spots on lower leaves
severity_rules.moderate: 10% - 30% coverage; coalescing angular black spots with marginal yellowing
severity_rules.severe: > 30% coverage; widespread defoliation, blighted stem lesions, and fruit scab formation

organic: Apply fixed copper sprays (Copper octanoate / Copper sulfate pentahydrate) mixed with Bacillus subtilis
Apply actigard (Acibenzolar-S-methyl) plant defense inducer where registered
chemical: Tank mix fixed copper fungicide (e.g., Kocide 3000) with Mancozeb (Mancozeb enhances copper bactericidal efficacy against copper-tolerant strains)
Apply streptomycin sulfate or kasugamycin under strict local agronomic regulatory approval

fertilizer: Discontinue high ammonium nitrate fertilizers; apply calcium nitrate and potassium sulfate
Foliar feed with zinc and manganese micronutrients to support plant immune enzymes
irrigation: Convert entirely to low-pressure drip irrigation; eliminate all overhead water splashing
Irrigate early in the morning so soil surface moisture evaporates rapidly
prevention: Use certified hot-water-treated seed (50°C for 25 minutes) to eradicate seedborne Xanthomonas
Rotate out of Solanaceous crops (tomatoes, peppers, potatoes, eggplants) for at least 2 to 3 years
Eradicate solanaceous weeds (such as black nightshade) that harbor bacterial populations
recovery_tips: Remove and destroy infected plants if detected early in small greenhouse setups
Sanitize stakes, trellises, and wire cages with 10% bleach solution before reuse

tomato_early_blight.description: Characterized by distinctive target-board or concentric circular rings within dark brown spots on older lower leaves. As spots enlarge, surrounding leaf tissue turns yellow, leading to premature drop and severe plant defoliation.
symptoms: Dark brown to black circular lesions displaying concentric 'target-board' rings
Surrounding foliar yellowing (chlorosis) that progresses outward from lesions
Early defoliation starting at the base of the vine and advancing upwards
Collar rot lesions at seedling stems and sunken leathery black spots at stem ends of fruits
causes: Moderate to warm temperatures (24-29°C) combined with high humidity, heavy dew, or overhead splashing
Overwintering fungal mycelium in solanaceous plant debris and contaminated soil
Stressed or nutrient-deficient plants with heavy fruit loads

severity_rules.mild: < 10% coverage; 2-3 target spots limited to bottom 2 branches
severity_rules.moderate: 10% - 30% coverage; multiple target spots across mid-canopy with yellow halos
severity_rules.severe: > 30% coverage; extensive defoliation, stem cankers, and fruit rot

organic: Foliar applications of copper hydroxide or liquid copper octanoate every 7-10 days
Spray Serenade Garden (Bacillus subtilis strain QST 713) or Regalia bio-fungicide
chemical: Apply protectant fungicides: Chlorothalonil (Bravo / Daconil) or Mancozeb
For active disease pressure, rotate with systemic fungicides: Azoxystrobin (Quadris), Boscalid (Endura), or Difenoconazole
Alternate FRAC codes (FRAC 11, 7, 3) to prevent resistance development

fertilizer: Maintain adequate nitrogen and potassium; plants deficient in N or K are dramatically more susceptible to Alternaria
Avoid excess nitrogen during vegetative phase to prevent soft, succulent tissue
irrigation: Drip irrigation strictly; eliminate water contact with foliage
Mulch soil around plants with 3 inches of clean straw or plastic mulch to form a barrier against soil spores
prevention: Plant early-blight tolerant cultivars (e.g., Mountain Supreme, Defiant PHR, Plum Regal)
Prune bottom 12-18 inches of leaves to prevent contact with soil
Enforce a 3-year crop rotation schedule away from tomatoes and potatoes
recovery_tips: Prune out infected lower leaves immediately upon sighting and seal in bags; do not compost
Thoroughly clean up and till or burn all crop residues at the conclusion of harvest

tomato_late_blight.description: One of the most destructive plant pathogens in history (cause of the Irish potato famine). Symptoms appear as large, irregular water-soaked pale green or greasy olive-brown lesions on leaves and stems. Under humid conditions, white fluffy mold develops on the undersides of leaves.
symptoms: Large, irregular water-soaked lesions that rapidly expand into dark brown or purplish-black blighted areas
Delicate white cottony/frosty mold (sporangiophores) appearing on leaf undersides during humid conditions
Dark brown greasy lesions running along petioles and main stems, leading to vine collapse
Firm, rough, golden-brown or mottled greasy rot on green and ripe fruits
causes: Cool, damp, fog-laden or rainy weather (15-22°C) with relative humidity above 90%
Wind-blown sporangia traveling miles from nearby infected tomato or potato fields
Infected potato tubers sprouting volunteer plants in spring

severity_rules.mild: < 10% coverage; isolated water-soaked dark blotches on upper leaf edges
severity_rules.moderate: 10% - 30% coverage; expanding necrotic blotches with visible white mold on undersides
severity_rules.severe: > 30% coverage; rapid systemic collapse of vine canopy, stem girdling, and fruit decay

organic: Immediate aggressive application of copper hydroxide (Kocide / Nu-Cop) at maximum label rates
Destroy severely blighted individual plants immediately to halt explosive spore generation
chemical: Apply targeted oomycete fungicides: Cyazofamid (Ranman), Mandipropamid (Revus), or Fluopicolide (Presidio)
Tank-mix systemic materials with protectants like Chlorothalonil or Mancozeb
Spray on a tight 5 to 7 day schedule when local late blight forecasting alerts trigger

fertilizer: Avoid heavy nitrogen inputs which fuel high canopy density and moisture retention
Ensure adequate potassium and silica to strengthen epidermal cell walls
irrigation: Drip irrigation only; irrigate early morning to ensure daytime dry-down
Ensure excellent field drainage to prevent localized pools of standing moisture
prevention: Plant certified late blight resistant cultivars possessing Ph-2 and Ph-3 resistance genes (e.g., Iron Lady, Mountain Magic, Defiant)
Destroy all volunteer potato and tomato plants in field margins in early spring
Sign up for regional late blight tracking alerts (such as USAblight or local university extension)
recovery_tips: Bag and remove infected plants during sunny dry afternoons to minimize spore dispersion during handling
Never leave culled diseased fruit or foliage in open piles near the production field

tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.description: A very common foliar fungal disease causing numerous small, circular spots (1-3 mm) with light tan to gray centers and dark brown margins. Inside older spots, tiny black specks (pycnidia fruiting bodies) are visible with a hand lens.
symptoms: Numerous small (1-3 mm), circular spots with grayish-white centers and distinct dark brown borders
Tiny black pinhead specks (pycnidia) clearly visible in center of mature spots
Infected leaves turn yellow around the spots, shrivel up, and drop off starting from the ground up
Unlike early blight, spots remain small and rarely display concentric rings; fruit infection is very rare
causes: Moderate temperatures (20-25°C) coupled with high humidity and rainfall
Fungal spores splashing from infected overwintering debris onto lower leaves
Overhead irrigation splashing water across dense foliar canopies

severity_rules.mild: < 10% coverage; tiny circular spots on the lowest 1-2 branch tiers
severity_rules.moderate: 10% - 30% coverage; heavy spotting and progressive yellowing across mid-canopy
severity_rules.severe: > 30% coverage; near complete lower and mid-canopy defoliation

organic: Copper sulfate or copper octanoate spray every 7-10 days starting at first spotting
Bio-fungicides like Bacillus subtilis or potassium bicarbonate sprays
chemical: Apply Chlorothalonil (Daconil 2787) or Mancozeb as preventative foliar sprays
Systemic triazole or strobilurin fungicides (e.g., Quadris or Flint) for severe pressure

fertilizer: Ensure steady balanced nutrition; defoliation is exacerbated in nitrogen-starved plants
Maintain calcium and potassium foliar balance
irrigation: Strict drip irrigation; never allow sprinklers to splash soil onto lower foliage
Apply thick organic or plastic mulch beneath plants to block spore splashing from soil
prevention: Prune the bottom 12-18 inches of foliage to keep leaves far away from soil splash
Sterilize plant supports and trellises before each growing season
Enforce 3-year crop rotation away from solanaceous plants
recovery_tips: Prune and discard infected bottom leaves as soon as first spots appear
Remove all crop residue at the end of the season and bury deeply or burn

tomato_yellow_leaf_curl.pathogen: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV, Begomovirus transmitted by Whiteflies)
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl.description: A severe viral disease transmitted exclusively by sweetpotato whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci). Infected plants exhibit marked stunting, upright erect shoot growth, and leaves that are drastically reduced in size, curled cupped upward, and showing intense interveinal yellowing (chlorosis).
symptoms: Leaves cupped upward and inward with prominent yellow (chlorotic) margins and interveinal areas
Severe reduction in leaf blade size, giving a stunted, crumpled, or 'bonsai' appearance
Marked plant stunting with shortened internodes and compact bushy growth
Flower trusses drop prematurely without setting fruit; overall yield can drop by 90-100%
causes: Feeding by the silverleaf / sweetpotato whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
Warm, dry climatic conditions promoting whitefly population explosions
Proximity to infected commercial or hobby tomato/pepper fields

severity_rules.mild: < 10% coverage; light marginal upward curling on newest terminal leaves
severity_rules.moderate: 10% - 30% coverage; pronounced cupping, yellow margins, and noticeable branch stunting
severity_rules.severe: > 30% coverage; total apical stunting, severe chlorosis, flower abortion, and zero fruit set

organic: Control whitefly vectors using insecticidal soaps, horticultural oils, or neem extract (azadirachtin)
Deploy yellow sticky traps (1 trap per 10-20 sq meters) to monitor and mass-trap whitefly adults
Introduce natural predators: Encarsia formosa parasitic wasps or Delphastus catalinae predatory beetles
chemical: There are no direct chemical viricides that cure a virus-infected plant; treatment targets whitefly vectors
Apply systemic neonicotinoid insecticides (such as Imidacloprid or Thiamethoxam) at transplanting
Foliar sprays of insect growth regulators (such as Pyriproxyfen or Spiromesifen) to break whitefly lifecycle

fertilizer: Supply balanced micronutrient foliar sprays (magnesium, iron, zinc) to relieve severe chlorotic stress
Maintain adequate potassium to assist in osmotic maintenance
irrigation: Maintain consistent soil moisture; water-stressed plants produce volatile compounds that attract whitefly vectors
Avoid dry stress spikes during flowering
prevention: Plant TYLCV-resistant or tolerant hybrids possessing the Ty-1, Ty-2, or Ty-3 resistance genes
Use UV-reflective silver plastic mulches to deter whiteflies from landing on young seedlings
Cover nursery seedlings with fine 50-mesh insect-proof netting for the first 30-40 days after germination
Maintain a 60-day host-free period between consecutive tomato crops
recovery_tips: Immediately rogue (uproot) and bag infected plants to prevent them from acting as viral reservoirs
Do not prune healthy plants immediately after handling virus-infected foliage without sanitizing hands

tomato_mosaic_virus.pathogen: Tomato Mosaic Virus (ToMV, Tobamovirus transmitted mechanically)
tomato_mosaic_virus.description: An exceptionally stable, mechanically transmitted tobamovirus. Infected tomato leaves develop distinctive alternating patches of light green and dark green (mosaic mottling), blistering, and distortion. In severe cases, leaflets develop a thin, spidery 'shoestring' or 'fern-leaf' appearance.
symptoms: Mottled pattern of light and dark green areas on leaves (mosaic pattern)
Leaf distortion including puckering, curling, blistered surfaces, and narrowing into shoestring shapes
Overall plant stunting and reduced fruit size with internal brown ring browning (internal necrosis)
Uneven fruit ripening with yellowish-brown blotchy patches on fruit walls
causes: Mechanical transmission through contaminated hands, pruning tools, stakes, or clothing during field operations
Infected seed coats or tobacco products (cigarettes, chewing tobacco) handled by field workers
Extremely persistent viral particles capable of surviving in dry plant debris and soil for multiple years

severity_rules.mild: < 10% coverage; faint light green/dark green mottling on young terminal leaflets
severity_rules.moderate: 10% - 30% coverage; clear mosaic distortion, leaf blistering, and minor shoestringing
severity_rules.severe: > 30% coverage; severe fern-leaf distortion, systemic vine stunting, and internal fruit necrosis

organic: There are no organic viricides to cure plant tissues once infected with ToMV
Spray 20% non-fat dry milk or skim milk solution onto workers' hands and tools during pruning (milk proteins bind and neutralize virus particles)
Promptly rogue out and destroy infected individual vines
chemical: No chemical viricides exist to cure plant viruses
Decontaminate all pruning shears, stakes, and greenhouse surfaces with 10% trisodium phosphate (TSP) or 20% bleach

fertilizer: Avoid excessive nitrogen that stimulates rapid abnormal cell growth in infected tissues
Maintain steady calcium and potassium nutrition
irrigation: Maintain uniform soil moisture using drip lines; avoid water fluctuations that stress vascular transport
prevention: Select resistant tomato cultivars bearing the Tm-1, Tm-2, or Tm-2^2 resistance genes
Strictly prohibit tobacco use (smoking, chewing) anywhere near greenhouse or field tomato plants
Require workers to wash hands thoroughly with soap and water or dip in milk solution before handling plants
Purchase certified virus-indexed seeds treated with trisodium phosphate (TSP) or dry heat (70°C for 4 days)
recovery_tips: Immediately remove infected plants: place carefully into bags inside the field to avoid rubbing healthy neighbors
Do not compost infected plant debris; burn or landfill discarded vines
Disinfect all stakes, cages, and wires with 10% TSP solution before re-staking next season
